content.title: In Rio's favelas, killing becomes a ritual
content.lead: Following the bloodiest police raid in Brazilian history, relatives speak of executions. While many citizens of Rio de Janeiro celebrate the police, the drug gangs continue as usual.

content.text: At the entrance to the Bairro 13 slum stands a burned-out car wreck. Next to it lie steel beams that, three days earlier, had served as a barricade against the police. The police had arrived to arrest Doca, who runs the operations of the Comando Vermelho (CV) drug gang in Rio de Janeiro's North Zone. After bloody clashes, the police later reported sixty dead drug criminals and four dead police officers that day. But this number quickly proved to be too low.

Behind the barricades lies a football pitch, the heart of the favela, as such slums are called in Rio. The morning after the police raid, the bodies found by residents in a forest further up the mountain were brought here. Fifty-seven dead, whose deaths the police had previously concealed. The bodies lay shoulder to shoulder on the street, their grieving relatives bent over them.

content.text: Now, two days later, the pools of blood have vanished. So has the police. The enraged locals would lynch any police officer who showed up here, says Adriana Odara of the Movimento Negro Unificado, a human rights organization representing the interests of the Afro-Brazilian population. She plans to show a group of journalists the wooded area on the mountain where the bodies were found today. But she's still waiting for permission. We'll see who's in charge up there hours later.

So, people wait at the community center next to the soccer field. Here, Fabiana Silva is explaining to relatives how they can gain access to the bodies. She works for a government agency that provides free legal aid. She says that the fact that the forensic medicine department is keeping the bodies sealed for so long is not standard procedure.

Relatives claim that the police executed the «boys,» as the rank-and-file fighters of the Comando Vermelho are called, in the forest, even though they had surrendered. «We don't deny that they belonged to the CV,» says one woman. «But executions are unacceptable.»

Activist Odara says they found many bodies with their hands bound behind their backs and gunshot wounds to the forehead and neck. Some had burn marks, indicating torture. Others had their torsos slashed open and their limbs severed; one body was also decapitated. Odara shows a photo of a police officer with a sword. Rio's police chief, however, claims the bodies were mutilated afterward to incriminate the police.

content.text: They are demanding an independent autopsy, as they don't trust the state medical examiners, says Odara. They also doubt the official figures – 117 dead and 113 arrested criminals. Local residents estimate the total number of dead to be 200, Odara says. There are still many missing persons, confirms legal advisor Fabiana Silva, without wanting to give exact figures.

Last Tuesday morning around 4:30 a.m., «Operation Containment» was launched with 2,500 officers. Police advanced into Complexo da Penha, a cluster of favelas named after the baroque Penha Church perched atop a hill, from several directions. Bairro 13 is part of this complex. Meanwhile, other units advanced into Complexo do Alemão on the opposite side of the hill.

According to police, the two favela complexes near the international airport are the CV headquarters in Rio and a training center for CV members from across Brazil. Up to ten tons of cocaine and at least fifty assault rifles are reportedly delivered here monthly and then distributed from here to other favelas controlled by the CV.

In the late 1970s, the Comando Vermelho (Red Command) was founded in a prison by drug criminals and left-wing opponents of the then-military dictatorship. This gave rise to a criminal gang that justified its actions as a fight for social justice. This explains the Robin Hood image that some members of the Red Command still have today. The CV supports imprisoned members and their families with drug money. Like Márcio Santos Nepomuceno, who has led the CV from prison for almost thirty years. His family considers him a political prisoner of the corrupt state.

content.text: In reality, Comando Vermelho runs a ruthless business. They are locked in a bitter struggle with the gangs Terceiro Comando and Amigos dos Amigos for control of Rio's favelas. For example, the day before the police raid, CV attacked a favela belonging to Terceiro Comando, killing two innocent civilians. However, Comando Vermelho's main adversaries are now militias formed by corrupt police officers and soldiers. Founded in the 1960s as vigilante groups, these militias are now also involved in drug trafficking, extortion, and, more recently, investing in the real estate market.

The many rival gangs make Rio a patchwork of organized crime. Rio's newspapers are almost daily filled with reports about politicians with ties to the gangs, and dozens of police officers have been dismissed in recent years because of their connections to the militias. This chaotic situation fuels speculation among the Cariocas, the residents of Rio. Is the far-right governor Cláudio Castro fighting the Comando Vermelho on behalf of the militias? And is the left-wing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva protecting the drug cartels?

In Rio, favela residents are always blamed for all the city's problems, says a local woman who wants to accompany us up the mountain. For her safety, we'll call her M. But the real masterminds of organized crime are outside the favelas. «How do the weapons and drugs get across borders and through checkpoints before being delivered here?» The guys here from Bairro 13 certainly couldn't handle such logistics.

Naming these masterminds would be dangerous, she says. They must have access to internal police information, in any case. «On the eve of the raid, everyone here in Bairro 13 knew the police were coming,» says M. That explains why the CV boss, Doca, was able to escape.

content.title: Armed men are waiting on the mountain

content.text: After two hours, the visit to the mountain is permitted. The journey continues by motorcycle, past roadblocks, and two kilometers up the road. «You have nothing to fear when God is on your side,» is written on a house wall. At an intersection, two horses stand in a pile of garbage. In the houses above the intersection, the «boys» put up fierce resistance that day. Now, three days later, armed youths are standing here again. «Please don't photograph them,» says M. The air smells of marijuana.

content.text: Videos circulating on social media show police storming the street known as Cabaré that morning. In the comments under the videos, they are hailed as heroes. «Only dead bandits are good bandits,» «The vagrants must die.» According to polls, two-thirds of Rio's residents support the police action; in the slums, approval is even higher.

Many yearn for a hardline policy like that practiced by El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, even though Bukele has suspended fundamental rights and carried out mass arrests in his country. «Direitos humanos,» or human rights, are merely an excuse used by left-wing politicians to protect bandits, one hears people say, even in Rio's slums.

The narrow streets of Cabaré are roofed with corrugated iron. But now the rain is dripping through everywhere. Police riddled the roofs with bullets from helicopters, says a gaunt figure collecting spent cartridges. All numbered, so by the police, he says, pointing to the bullet holes in his house: «God protected me.»

image.caption: «Penha belongs to Christ»: a religious message amidst a war zone. From helicopters, police riddled the corrugated iron roof of the Cabaré street with rifle bullets.

content.text: Across the street, three bullet holes are visible in the front door of an elderly woman's house. The police had been searching for bandits in a corner building, but that wasn't their area. She had known the «boys» since she was a child, and they had always respected her. The recent press reports that they demanded protection money from them were untrue. On the contrary, the woman says, the «boys» were always there for her when she needed help. Unlike the state, which sends the police to kill people here, M. adds.

The corner house the police were looking for is located one street over. Thirty armed men climbed in through a window and barricaded themselves in her living room, a 36-year-old woman recounts. «War will be met with war,» the police officers who surrounded the house shouted. She negotiated with the police for the «guys» to surrender. «Otherwise, the police would have stormed our house and killed them all,» she says.

Her house and the small restaurant next door were riddled with bullets. She didn't know if the refrigerators and ovens still worked. The police officers had stuffed their bags with drinks from her refrigerators and moved on.

Above Cabaré Street, a concrete staircase built into the hillside leads into the forest. Police drone footage shows the uniformed «boys,» armed with automatic rifles, fleeing down it that day. Straight into a deadly trap. Special forces approaching from the other side of the mountain had long since cut off the route into the Complexo do Alemão. Now the «boys» were surrounded.

content.text: Residents later found the 57 bodies in the forest. A few camouflage uniforms, shoes, and backpacks lying on the forest floor bear witness to the carnage. Bloodstains are visible on rocks, and bandages are scattered about.

«We couldn't go any further up the mountain,» M. said. Why remained unclear. There's a quarry up there, rumored to be a hideout for the Comando Vermelho. Locals said the police had dumped more bodies in a nearby ravine. But the area was inaccessible without mountaineering equipment. So we had to turn back. On the way down, we passed young men with machine guns and radios.

A protest march has gathered on the football field down in Bairro 13. Left-wing politicians and human rights activists are giving interviews. Flags bearing the names of Karl Marx and Che Guevara are visible, as are demonstrators wearing Palestinian scarves and Islamic Jihad T-shirts. Chants against the governor ring out repeatedly: «Cláudio Castro is a murderer!»

A TV helicopter circles overhead. In a restaurant around the corner, the patrons are glued to the television, which shows an aerial view of their neighborhood. The program displays images of the protest alongside videos of the fighting from three days ago. Bandits who made life hell for honest citizens were killed, the presenter rants. A group of young men, undisturbed by this, are having their lunch. They have propped their rifles against the wall next to the table.

content.text: While the protest march moves through Bairro 13, shots are fired a few kilometers away in another favela, where the Comando Vermelho and the Terceiro Comando are fighting. On a city highway, an innocent 28-year-old woman in the back seat of her taxi is fatally struck in the head by a stray bullet. Three days after Rio de Janeiro made history with Brazil's bloodiest police raid, the city has returned to normal.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- A police raid in Rio's favelas resulted in at least 117 deaths and 113 arrests, though locals claim there were up to 200 deaths and accuse the police of executions and torture.
- The raid targeted Comando Vermelho, one of Brazil's most powerful drug cartels, known for drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and violent conflicts with rival groups and militias.
- The situation remains tense, with residents demanding independent investigations as debates over violence, corruption, and the state's role persist.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
A police raid in Rio's favelas has resulted in at least 117 deaths and 113 arrests. Residents, however, speak of up to 200 dead and accuse the police of executions and torture.
 The raid targeted Comando Vermelho, one of Brazil's most powerful drug cartels. The group is responsible for drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and armed conflicts with rival groups and militias.
 - The situation on the ground remains tense, with residents demanding independent investigations, while the debate about violence, corruption and the role of the state continues.

playableVideoTeasers.title: NZZ Format | Europe's new cocaine front – how drug gangs are infiltrating Spain's coastal towns
playableVideoTeasers.description: For years, cocaine use has been rising in Europe, generating lucrative business for criminal gangs. Now, southern Spain is becoming an increasingly important hub for smugglers. For the people in the tranquil coastal towns, this has sometimes had dramatic consequences. Many tourists appreciate Andalusia for its stunning beaches, idyllic villages, and cozy tapas bars. But Europe's southernmost region also has another face: Here, criminal gangs are expanding, supplying all of Europe with cocaine. «We have a veritable drug economy here,» says social worker Alma Jugado. Andalusia is one of the poorest regions in Spain. Drug smugglers here earn more in a single night than others do in a month. So-called TikTok narcos—influencers who portray the smuggler's life as a big party—contribute to the popularity of the illegal trade. Law enforcement is forced to conduct increasingly dangerous operations while simultaneously becoming increasingly powerless. The documentary delves deep into Andalusia's smuggling business. She accompanies customs officers, social workers – and an investigative journalist who wants to meet with one of the masterminds behind the drug gangs. It becomes clear that the rising crime in southern Spain is far more than a local problem.

playableVideoTeasers.title: NZZ Format | Europe's new drug crisis? How fentanyl and other synthetic opioids threaten us
playableVideoTeasers.description: Highly potent synthetic opioids have killed thousands of people in North America. Now they are appearing in Europe, putting local drug policies to the test. When fentanyl emerged in Vancouver, there was hardly any warning. Within a few years, it largely displaced heroin from the illegal drug market, and the number of fatal overdoses rose dramatically. «I pray that Europe doesn't end up in the same situation as us,» says Canadian addiction specialist Paxton Bach. «But I fear it's only a matter of time.» Meanwhile, highly potent synthetic opioids like Nitazene are also spreading in Europe. They are sold online, mixed with heroin or pills, and sometimes consumed without the users' knowledge. Even the smallest excess can trigger a fatal overdose. In Germany, the fundamental changes in the drug market are becoming apparent. Clinics are increasingly treating younger users; at the same time, the trade is shifting from the streets to the internet. The substances can be ordered with just a few clicks via social networks, messaging apps, and online shops. This makes it harder to reach users with traditional support services and to identify new developments in the market. Since the dismantling of the open drug scenes at Zurich's Platzspitz and Letten districts, Switzerland has been considered a global model of pragmatic drug policy. Supervised consumption sites, substitution programs, drug checking, and early warning systems are intended to prevent isolated incidents from escalating into new crises. But can this successful model of the 1990s withstand a globalized, synthetic drug market?
